records.name: Vilonija
records.facts_used: For Vilonija, Siliņš’s dictionary points to Greek philon, a dear one or object of love. This is a gloss of the separate Greek word within the name’s origin account. It does not require inventing a new literal translation of the entire personal name. The catalogue documents Vilonija in Jasmuiža in 1925, referring to page 328 of the dictionary. This supplies a concrete place and year in Latvian personal-name history. It does not mean that the name was invented in Jasmuiža or establish a separate year of calendar inclusion.

records.uncertainties: Exact p.328 Greek-word gloss and Jasmuiža1925 record; do not confuse with a place-origin or manufacture a whole-name meaning.

records.name: Vilora
records.facts_used: Vilora is a documented Latvian rendering of Russian Вилора. Melnikov’s Russian-name dictionary explains Вилора through the initials of a phrase naming V. I. Lenin as organiser of the revolution. This describes a political naming mechanism rather than the beliefs of every Latvian bearer’s family. Vrublevskaya’s 2017 study places Вилора among formations of the 1920s–1930s, citing Suprun. The Latvian Language Agency separately supports Vilora with page 184 of the 1993 rendering manual. These establish the Russian name’s historical context and a Latvian spelling correspondence, not its first registration in Latvia.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicitly scoped international family evidence supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Inspected exact LVA pair and dissertation PDF126/printed126. Melnikov’s expansion is attributed rather than universal. Do not infer a Latvian family’s ideology, a first Latvian attestation or an original Veliev claim: old.vspu.ru DNS fails, modern replacement404.

records.name: Cecilija
records.facts_used: Cecilija is connected with the Roman family name Caecilius, based on Latin caecus, blind. The feminine form belongs to an old Latin family continued in Christian naming. The historical root meaning does not describe any particular bearer’s eyesight or character. The 1964 Tikiu Dievą calendar, reprinted by Salys in 1983, gives Cecilija with short form Cilė on 22 November. This directly records the full and short names together in print. The calendar’s publication year is neither the name’s creation date nor the date of its first Lithuanian bearer.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicitly scoped international family evidence supports two paragraphs in five languages.

records.name: Cilė
records.facts_used: Cilė is a Lithuanian short form of Cecilė or Cecilija, explicitly identified by Luca Pavan in his study of Lithuanian/Italian name resemblances. Through the full name it belongs to Latin Caecilius and caecus, blind. Resemblance to the Italian name of Chile does not explain its origin. The 1964 Tikiu Dievą calendar, reprinted in 1983, already places Cilė in parentheses beside Cecilija on 22 November. Pavan’s 2014 article discusses this shortening in a different context, language learning. Both sources show concrete use of the form rather than its invention.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicitly scoped international family evidence supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Pavan Verbum5(2014),pp238–246,PDF6/printed243 exact Cilė→Cecilė/Cecilija; PDF5/printed242 table visually inspected. Exact guide Cilė404.

records.name: Cecilia
records.facts_used: Cecilia is connected with the Roman family name Caecilius, based on Latin caecus, blind. The feminine form belongs to an old Latin family continued in Christian naming. Frances Burney’s 1782 novel Cecilia, or Memoirs of an Heiress centres on fictional heiress Cecilia Beverley. Its first chapter already connects her inheritance with keeping her surname on marriage. This is an English literary example of the exact name, not the first Cecilia in Estonia.

records.name: Silja
records.facts_used: Silja is a short form of Cecilia explicitly identified for both Finnish and Estonian by the international name guide. records.name: Silje
records.facts_used: Nordic name guides explain Silje as a short form of Cecilie or Cecilia, continuing the Latin Caecilius family and caecus, blind. The Norwegian and Danish accounts establish an international family connection rather than one compulsory borrowing route for every Estonian family. Norwegian singer Silje Nergaard’s official biography dates her debut single Tell Me Where You’re Going to 1990 and records Pat Metheny’s participation. This gives the exact name a concrete Norwegian cultural episode. It is not Silje’s first recorded use in Estonia.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicitly scoped international family evidence supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Nordic exact-form origin, explicitly Norwegian dated bearer example; no claim of first Estonian use or shared counts.

records.name: Sille
records.facts_used: Norwegian name scholar Gulbrand Alhaug identifies Sille as an affectionate form of Cecilie; the international guide also calls it a Danish diminutive of Cecilia. Alhaug’s historical account places nineteenth-century use of Sille chiefly in Vest-Agder, Norway, while warning that the underlying data also include spelling variants such as Cille. This regional history provides Nordic context rather than an exact Sille-only count or a first Estonian record.
